answer_1.quote: We systematically evaluate automatic metrics for text generation, assessing their effectiveness and reliability for non-English languages by assessing the correlation with human scores.

answer_2.quote: We assess a total of 10 evaluation metrics that are common in evaluating abstractive summarization: N-Gram Metrics: measure the lexical overlap between the system and reference summaries. For this evaluation, we used ROUGE, considering four variants: ROUGE-1 (unigram), ROUGE-2 (bigram), ROUGE-3 (trigram), ROUGE-L (longest common subsequence). We also use CHRF measuring the character n-gram F-score; and BLEU.

answer_3.quote: We also used Gemini as a Judge - with the Gemini model 1.0-pro as an evaluator, in which the given prompt was in the same format as the one given to the annotators.
methods: prompting of Gemini to assess quality without any parameter updates

answer_4.quote: We engaged human annotators to evaluate summaries generated by large language models (LLMs). Our data collection evaluates document summaries in eight languages... we hired annotators through Amazon Mechanical Turk (MTurk)... each model-generated summary was ranked by three different participants.
answer_4.guideline: The annotator evaluates each summary using 1-4 Likert scale along two quality dimensions: coherence, which assesses the summaries' grammaticality and readability, and completeness, which measures the degree to which they capture the text's main ideas.
